title: Jujutsu (jj)
q3_concrete_actions: 3.1 — Op-log record type `OpRecord` stores `pre_root` alongside `post_root` plus `parents[]`, so undo of a `local` or `shared-append` operation is a root-pointer move, not an inverse-patch application. Falsified by G1.3 (HARD): 0 failures over >=100k in-process and >=1000 CLI property-generated command sequences, coverage-gated.

3.1 — Every `OpRecord` carries a typed `class` field partitioning operations into `local` / `shared-append` / `shared-destructive`. `ltx undo` refuses a `shared-destructive` operation and instead emits a signed retraction that is itself a new logged operation. This is the design jj issue #9707 requested (open 2026-06-26, zero maintainer comments) and has not received.

3.2 — `ltx sync` maintains a bridge anchor table keyed `git-commit-id -> change-id`, reconciled on every fetch, with content-similarity re-anchoring when a plain-Git teammate strips the header (jj's `change-id` header survives `git commit --amend` but explicitly not `git rebase`). Measured by G3.2 (SOFT, >=99% change-ID and provenance recovery across >=500 simulated PR flows) and G3.3 (HARD, 0 observable anomalies in the Git-only teammate suite); unrecoverable cases are logged lossy edges under G3.4, not silent misses.

3.3 — ADR-1 (merge model) adopts jj's odd-tree `A+(C-B)` conflict representation and the `Merge::flatten`/`Merge::simplify` identities wholesale, and must pin the criss-cross topology of jj bug #6369 as a named test case in the G0.3 merge-replay corpus.
3.3 — Every same-change auto-resolution is written as a typed resolution event in the op log, so jj's documented lossy case stays reconstructible rather than silent.

3.4 — Conflict materialize/parse round-trips must be byte-exact: jj #9868 (materialize -> parse dropping a trailing `\r`) is classified as a G1.2 (HARD, target 0) byte-fidelity violation, and the G1.2 adversarial corpus must carry CRLF-terminated conflict sides explicitly.

3.5 — All content goes through FastCDC-family content-defined chunking with BLAKE3 addressing, with parameters fixed by ADR-2 (chunk parameters) against measurement rather than library defaults. Gated by G1.8 (SOFT/perf: p95 new bytes for a 1-byte edit in a 50MB file < 262,144 over 100 trials x 5 file types) and G1.9 (SOFT/perf, dual baseline: store must come in under restic x 1.25 AND git-gc x 1.5 simultaneously).

3.6 — Retention is per-durability-tier: checkpointed objects are structurally ineligible for collection, and every autosnapshot thinning is itself an op-log entry. Gated by G2.8 (HARD): 0 checkpointed objects collected and 0 thinnings absent from the op log, over year-long traces.

3.6 — Tier policy must also cover collection of unreachable index tables, which jj lacks entirely (`There's no garbage collection of unreachable tables yet`); this is currently outside G2.8's scope and needs a registry addition.

3.7 — Lenses ship as shareable, versioned structural projection objects (no jj analogue: templates format output, revsets select commits), gated by G2.7 (HARD, 0 information-loss or reconstruction failures over >=10,000 generated cases) and G3.6 (SOFT, 100% of Git publishes lens-defined with every rewrite-desire incident logged).

3.8 — Ed25519-signed provenance attaches to checkpoints, which are addressable objects, structurally sidestepping the blocker von Zweigbergk named in jj #8166 ('Git notes can only be attached to existing objects (and we don't model changes as Git objects)'). Gated by G5.1 (HARD, 0 incorrect provenance query results on a >=1000-checkpoint ground-truth suite), G5.2 (HARD, 0 undetected attestation tampering) and G5.4 (SOFT, `ltx trace --agent --unreviewed --touching <path>` p95 < 200ms).

3.9 — Lattice v1 omits jj roadmap items explicitly: no VFS, no cloud repo server or caching daemon, no forge-submit commands, no submodules, and no backend-level copy tracking — copy/rename is derived from the non-authoritative semantic index, gated by G4.7 (HARD, 0 query divergences after index delete-and-regenerate).

3.9 — A single store backend is chosen by benchmark under ADR-3 (store backend) instead of jj's pluggable-backend abstraction, whose cost is visible in `SimpleBackend` remaining a perpetual proof of concept while only `GitBackend` is production-ready.

3.9 — G1.4 (HARD, 8 workspaces x 10,000 ops) must fuzz the change-ID and provenance indexes, not only the content store, and must include a filesystem that does not honour locks — the exact configuration in which jj #2193's change-ID index corruption occurs.
uncomfortable_findings: jj's documented lossy auto-resolution is a MERGE bug, not a rebase bug — so 'lenses replace rebase' does not dodge it. The draft framed jj bug #6369 as the rebase-onto-same-change-and-back case from the docs. #6369's actual title is 'A crisscross merge leads to losing changes' and its reproduction is E = merge(merge(A,B), merge(A,B)) recovering pre-change content, with no rebase anywhere in it. Lattice deletes rebase but KEEPS merges and makes them non-blocking, which means it inherits this loss class in full and arguably increases exposure to it. 'No checkpointed data is ever lost' must be reconciled with an auto-resolution rule that is knowingly lossy in exactly the topology Lattice makes cheapest. G6.1's data-loss hunter must be aimed at criss-cross topologies specifically or it will not find this class at all.

G1.5's 100ms target is the exact number jj's own contributors set as 'acceptable' in August 2023 and have not reached in three years, while doing strictly less work per file than Lattice plans to. arxanas profiled `jj status` on nixpkgs WITH Watchman at 768ms (snapshot 257ms, conflicts 424ms) and wrote 'I think we could get status down to an acceptable ~100ms'. In March 2025 a fresh `jj git clone` of zed still measured `jj st` at 1.207s. Lattice adds continuous autosnapshotting AND per-file CDC chunking on top of the same scan. G1.5 and G1.6 are SOFT and will be the first waived — and waiving them removes the only measured defence of the model's usability.

G1.5's 'watcher resident' premise is not safe: a filesystem watcher does not help when the cost is index/ref import, which is precisely where Lattice's load is larger than jj's. On JetBrains/kotlin (~55k Git refs + ~44k jj refs) in October 2025, `jj log` took 2.8s vs 0.8s with `--ignore-working-copy`; the reporter states 'Enabling watchman did not really change the timing' and that `git pack-refs` helped more. Lattice's op log plus provenance index is a strictly larger per-command load than jj's refs, so the resident-watcher assumption baked into G1.5's metric may not buy what the gate assumes.

The one 2025 performance win in jj that the draft cited does not apply to Lattice's bottleneck. `git.subprocess = true` cut fetch 38.070s -> 8.889s and push 1:25.79 -> 22.600s, but the reporting user had `core.fsmonitor = watchman` enabled in BOTH columns: the fix replaced libgit2 on NETWORK paths and left working-copy snapshot cost untouched. There is no comparable win available for the snapshot path, which is the path Lattice makes heavier.

CDC for a VCS has been a specified, wanted request in jj since 2024-01-22 (#2865, citing the FastCDC paper directly) and is unimplemented 2.5 years later; the roadmap's entire commitment is one sentence. The blocker is not ignorance — CDC-chunked content is not representable in a Git object model. Lattice claims BOTH universal CDC AND a Git bridge that ships FIRST. jj's history is direct evidence those two constraints fight each other.

Conflicts leak across the Git bridge in practice, and AI agents are the named vector. jj needed a non-standard `jj:trees` header PLUS decoy `.jjconflict-base-*/`/`.jjconflict-side-*/` directories, and conflict commits still reached the real public Ghostty repository because someone used plain `git` to bypass jj's checks (#9571, 2026-05-28) — an issue that explicitly names 'AI agents' as a likely cause. Lattice's agent population is larger by design, its byte-fidelity promise (G1.2) is stricter, and G3.3's target is 0 anomalies.

Stable change IDs do not survive plain-Git tooling, so 'change identity survives what teammates do' requires a lossy heuristic. jj's `change-id` header is preserved by `git commit --amend` and explicitly NOT by `git rebase`. 'Plain-Git teammates notice nothing' (G3.3) is achievable; identity survival is not, without content-similarity re-anchoring — which is why G3.2's target is 99% and not 100%, and why the residual 1% must be enumerated in the G3.4 lossy-edge ledger rather than absorbed silently.

The seven-noun budget (G2.3, HARD, 0 violations) is the least credible gate in the registry, and unlike the perf gates it cannot be waived. jj launched with the same minimalist ambition and now ships change, commit, revision, operation, view, workspace, bookmark, conflict, divergent change, hidden commit, change offset, evolog, revset, fileset, template and immutable set; its own advocates document terminology inconsistency (discussion #4285: 'the documentation uses the terms changes and commits inconsistently'), and the FAQ's very first entry exists to explain a noun's behaviour. Lattice must additionally hide changesets, durability tiers, provenance, redaction, attestations and the op log behind seven nouns.

G3.6's 100% lens-defined publishes emits force-push effects into a forge whose model Lattice does not control. A lens-generated Git history re-derives commit IDs whenever the lens or the underlying record changes; to GitHub that is a force-push — the exact failure in discussion #4285. Lattice has removed force-push from its own vocabulary while still producing its consequences in someone else's system. G3.6 is correctly SOFT in gates.toml; the spec prose asserting the capability should be softened to match.

`ltx undo` cannot undo a sync, and calling it undo is a category error jj already hit. Per jj's own teaching material, undoing a push 'doesn't tell the remote to restore its previous state, the remote is left intact', producing conflicted bookmarks and divergent change IDs on the next fetch or push; jj states that in future `jj undo` 'may outright refuse to undo operations that interacted with the remote'. Lattice's signed retraction is a better answer but is a COMPENSATING action, not an undo — G1.3 must not be allowed to score it as one.

Lock-freedom is not free, and the weak link is the index, not the store — which is worse for Lattice than for jj. jj #2193 (open since 2023-09-01) shows the change-ID index relying on locks that are unavailable when a repo is synced via rsync or Dropbox, allowing index corruption with `jj debug reindex` as the only recovery. Note the scope correction: this is a distributed-filesystem hazard, not a general local one — but it is exactly the configuration jj's concurrency design advertises as supported. Lattice's provenance index is a strictly larger, more complex sidecar than jj's StackedTable, so G1.4 must fuzz the index under a lock-less filesystem.

jj's identity sidecar has no garbage collection at all, and Lattice's equivalent is bigger — with no gate covering it. The architecture doc states plainly: 'There's no garbage collection of unreachable tables yet.' G2.8 governs checkpointed objects and autosnapshot thinning, not index-table growth. Lattice's provenance index is strictly larger than jj's StackedTable, so unbounded index growth is currently an ungated failure mode in the registry.

The resourcing picture is worse than 'the creator joined a startup': a funded company now owns a large bloc of jj upstream, and its mission statement is Lattice's differentiator. `docs/paid_contributors.md` lists East River Source Control FIRST, ahead of Alphabet/Google, with eight jj contributors (martinvonz, ilyagr, thoughtpolice, steveklabnik, benbrittain, davidbarsky, ConnerPetzold, bts). ERSC's own site describes it as 'creating the building blocks for human <-> machine collaboration' — not merely a storage layer. jj's roadmap previously carried no dates because 'most people contributing to Jujutsu do so in their spare time'; that constraint has now been lifted for jj by capital and has not been lifted for Lattice.

jj is already moving into Lattice's agent-native differentiator with the right people engaged. #8166 (per-revision metadata, open 2025-11-28) has von Zweigbergk actively engaged and a commenter explicitly asking for prompts attached to changes so a model upgrade can drive a 'prompt rebase'; #9561 asks for native agent-session syncing; #9814 (agent-friendly non-interactive interfaces for split/squash/diffedit/restore) was opened and closed within a day. Lattice's agent-native lead is measured in months of design, not years.

Adoption arithmetic is discouraging even in the best case, and the draft overstated the elapsed time. The ~900 internal Google users figure comes from the JJ Con 2025 keynote (held 2025-09-28, Sunnyvale) — roughly six years after a late-2019 start, not seven. jj had every structural advantage Lattice is counting on (creator full-time at Google, invisible Git interop as the on-ramp) and reached that number. The figure remains secondary and unverified against the primary talk.

Two jj roadmap items Lattice declares non-goals are the very mechanisms jj identifies as the fix for problems Lattice will have. jj's roadmap justifies a VFS partly because it 'can also make it cheap to snapshot the working copy by keeping track of all changes compared to the base commit' — the exact cost Lattice increases and then rules out the remedy for. And jj's copy-tracking design leaves recording to the backend specifically because detection 'would be too slow' on very large repos, which is a direct challenge to Lattice deriving copy/rename from a non-authoritative semantic index.

User demand documented in jj's own FAQ cuts against two Lattice design choices. The FAQ carries 'Can I prevent Jujutsu from recording my unfinished work? I'm not ready to commit it.' — direct pressure against no-staging-area continuous autosnapshotting — and both 'Can I interactively create a new commit from only some of the changes...like git add -p' and 'Is there something like git rebase --interactive'. Users of a working-copy-as-commit VCS still ask for staging semantics and for interactive history editing; Lattice answers both with new nouns (changesets, lenses) that must fit inside the seven-noun budget.

title: Mercurial changeset evolution
q3_concrete_actions: ADR-LENS-001: a lens MUST NOT contain per-checkpoint entries; lens rules are predicates over checkpoint attributes, so lens size is O(rules) not O(rewrites).
Gate G-LENS-SIZE: generate 100,000 checkpoints under a fixed lens; assert serialized lens bytes are constant and cold-start p99 of `ltx log --lens` is independent of checkpoint count.

Gate G-OPLOG-INDEX (split out from G-LENS-SIZE): for bounded queries (`ltx trace --agent --unreviewed --touching src/auth/`, `ltx undo`, sync discovery closure) the test harness counts records deserialized and asserts the count is bounded by answer size, not history length, at 10^2 / 10^4 / 10^6 operations.

ADR-STORE-001: index-backed op-log and lineage reads are an ADMISSION requirement on the redb/RocksDB-vs-append-only-packs benchmark — a backend without indexed prefix and secondary-index lookup is disqualified before throughput is measured, not traded off.
ADR-SYNC-001: sync discovery negotiates over a stable subdivision of the checkpoint DAG (obshashrange's insight), never per-node hashes that an ancestor write can invalidate.

Gate G-SYNC-DISCOVERY: replay the CEDObsmarkersExchange pathological cases — (a) append one operation referencing an ancient checkpoint then sync, asserting bytes-on-wire and round trips are O(delta) not O(history); (b) superset case where peer B holds a strict superset of A's operations, asserting A→B transfers zero payload bytes.

Gate G-SYNC-LOUD: no `obshashrange.max-revs`-style silent protocol disable ships; a build where discovery can fall back without writing a `discovery-degraded` operation into the op log fails the gate.

Lens evaluator returns a three-valued Rust enum per checkpoint — Present, HiddenByRule, UnresolvableLocally — with no Default impl so call sites cannot silently collapse the third case; `ltx log` renders UnresolvableLocally distinctly and never folds it into hidden.

Gate G-PARTIAL: clone with a truncated chunk/op set and assert no checkpoint is reported hidden when the actual cause is missing local data; the same three-valued discipline is mandatory for op-log replay and tombstone application.
Lenses have no authority over durability tier: a lens can never remove a published checkpoint from the record and tier transitions are never expressible as lens rules.
Gate G-LENS-READONLY: property test over generated repositories asserting `ltx internals digest R` is byte-identical with lens L applied, absent, or deleted.
Gate G-NOUNS: lint every user-facing help string and error message in `ltx`; fail the build on any noun outside the seven plus an explicit allowlist whose diff requires ADR-level review.

Gate G-DIVERGE: two checkpoints carrying one change ID construct a first-class divergence object surfaced by `ltx trace` and `ltx log` and resolvable only by a later checkpoint; a build that can produce two visible checkpoints with one change ID and no divergence object fails. Ships in v1 alongside conflicts.

ADR-LINEAGE-001: create the change-lineage store the spec is missing — uniform 1-to-1 typed edges (predecessor, successor, kind, group_id) with kind in {amend, split, fold, prune, converge}; arity carries no meaning; multi-part relations use group_id + index. This REPLACES the draft's recommendation to copy Mercurial's marker-arity discrimination.

Gate G-LINEAGE-ARITY: a split of A into B and C, and two independent amendments of A into B and C, must produce structurally distinct, non-inferable lineage records under every interleaving and partial-replication order.

ADR-OPLOG-001: the operation log is a DAG of operations over repo-state views (jj's operation/view model), not a linear Merkle chain; concurrent heads are reconciled by a defined 3-way view merge that is itself a logged operation; 'append-only' means no operation is ever removed, not that the log is totally ordered.
Gate G-OPLOG-MERGE: run N concurrent operations across two workspaces and one remote; assert the merged view is order-independent and `ltx undo` from the merged head is well-defined.

ADR-PROV-001: the provenance effect-flag bitfield (description / content / parent / actor / task-link changed) lives in the provenance record's fixed, indexed header; storing it in a key/value metadata blob is forbidden — this is the specific mistake `obsutil.EFFECTFLAGFIELD` made.

ADR-REDACT-001: redaction tombstones record the pre-image's parent links (Mercurial v1 marker parent field) so Merkle structure survives content removal, and tombstone propagation uses a push-based, acknowledged protocol with explicit per-peer confirmation rather than discovery negotiation.
Gate G-REDACT-ACK: `ltx internals redaction-status` reports unconfirmed peers indefinitely and never reports a redaction complete on quorum or timeout.

ADR-BRIDGE-001 + Gate G-BRIDGE-LENS: every Git-bridge export embeds the lens ID and lens content hash in a commit trailer, and `ltx sync` refuses to extend a Git branch whose last export names a different lens hash without an explicit, logged operation.
Gate G-UNDO-LOCAL: the undo gate measures local invertibility only; every operation type carries a `locally-undoable | externally-visible` classification rendered by the CLI.
Gate G-THIN: property test asserting the set of checkpoint-tier and published-tier objects is byte-identical before and after every generated autosnapshot thinning run.
uncomfortable_findings: LATTICE NEEDS AN OBSOLESCENCE STORE AND DOES NOT HAVE ONE. 'Changes carry stable IDs surviving amendment' means an amendment produces a new checkpoint bearing an existing change ID. The predecessor→successor relation between them is a WRITE-PATH fact that peers must exchange to agree on what supersedes what. That is precisely obsstore. Lenses are read-path and cannot express it. None of Lattice's seven nouns names it and the spec does not specify it. The spec's cleanest differentiator — read-path-only history shaping — is currently resting on an unspecified write-path store that has Mercurial's exact fourteen-year exchange problem.

THE OP LOG MUST BE A DAG, NOT A CHAIN — the spec's phrasing ('append-only Merkle-linked OPERATION LOG') describes a linear chain, which cannot converge. Mercurial's obsmarkers are a SET: union merges cleanly, which is why hg could defer discovery for a decade without a correctness bug. A Merkle-linked chain has no union operation; two workspaces or a peer sync produce two heads that cannot both extend one chain. jj — whose change IDs Lattice borrows — solved this by making the operation log a commit-DAG analogue ('each commit object is instead an operation and each tree object is instead a view'; 'normally linear... non-linear if there are divergent operations') and 3-way-merging divergent view objects. Lattice inherits the harder version of hg's problem, not the easier one.

MERCURIAL'S OWN SUCCESSOR FORMAT ABANDONS MARKER-ARITY DISCRIMINATION, so 'steal it verbatim' is the wrong recommendation. Arity never worked for fold: `createmarkers` rejects multi-predecessor relations ('Fold markers can only have 1 successors') and emits N one-to-one markers with out-of-band `fold-id`/`fold-idx`/`fold-size` metadata. It needed a correctness fix for split twelve years in — hg-evolve 11.1.6, 2024-11-27: 'unrelated parts of splits are no longer considered content-divergent'. And CEDObsstoreFormat's V3 plan states: 'Current plan would be to unify on 1-1 markers. It seems simpler, and more extensible.' Lattice should adopt typed 1-1 lineage edges, not arity encoding.

THE EFFECT-FLAG PRECEDENT IS A WARNING, NOT A TEMPLATE. Mercurial's v1 marker header contains a uint16 bit field explicitly 'reserved for flags used in common obsolete marker operations, to avoid repeated decoding of metadata entries' — and the effect flags are NOT in it. They are written as decimal ASCII into the opaque key/value metadata blob, behind the comment 'we plan to extend the existing obsmarkers bit-field when the effect flag design will be stabilized.' Nine years later it is still stranded, so answering 'which amendments only touched the description?' still costs a full obsstore parse. `ltx trace --agent --unreviewed --touching src/auth/` will have exactly this failure mode unless the bitfield is in an indexed fixed header from day one.

MARKER EXCHANGE DISCOVERY IS UNSOLVED AFTER FOURTEEN YEARS AND LATTICE'S NATIVE SYNC WALKS INTO IT. hg's first algorithm (obshashtree) resent everything on superset mismatch ('detected as different markers on both side and the source will send everything to the destination again' — a case the wiki says 'will be very common') and cascade-invalidated whole subtrees. The replacement obshashrange is STILL not in core: hg-evolve 12.0.0's obsdiscovery.py is headed 'Status: Experiment in progress // open question.' It ships TWO escape hatches — `experimental.obshashrange.max-revs` ('automatically disable... ensuring no large repository will get affected'; the wire capability is simply not advertised) and `evolution.obsdiscovery = no` recommended 'For very large repositories'. The optimized path is documented as not scaling.

STORAGE IMPROVEMENT IS BLOCKED ON EXCHANGE, NOT INDEPENDENT OF IT. q3_concrete_actions: ADR-1 resolves to a checkpoint DAG over Merkle directory trees plus structural three-way merge, and its decision text must state explicitly that Lattice buys Git round-trip fidelity by giving up native order-independence, recovering it only where gate G2.1 certifies it.

G2.1 property 1 (commutativity), restated to be well-typed: normalise(merge(base,a,b)) == normalise(merge(base,b,a)), where normalise maps a conflict object to its unordered set of side-blobs plus base. The prior 'byte equality of merged trees' assertion is withdrawn because conflict-marker output is legitimately side-ordered.

G2.1 property 2 (grouping-independence), restated as Pijul states it: applying {B,C} to A in one operation yields the same checkpoint tree as applying B then C. The prior formulation merge(a, merge(b,c)) == merge(merge(a,b), c) is withdrawn as ill-typed for three-way merge, since the three operands do not share a base.
G2.1 property 3: resolving a conflict object yields the same checkpoint regardless of which side arrived first.

ADR-1 acceptance criteria: a full G2.1 run of 10^5 cases must complete within a fixed CI wall-clock budget (proposed 20 minutes on the reference runner), and resolving a checkpoint carrying k accumulated unresolved conflict objects must be at worst quadratic in k. The prior 'sub-quadratic in conflicting-change count' requirement is withdrawn — darcs-3 achieved quadratic and judged it testable, and history depth is not the complexity parameter of a snapshot three-way merge.
Pijul's G/X reshuffle enters LTX-MERGE's fixture set as fixture/gx-reshuffle, asserted identically under structural merge and under the line-merge fallback.

Lattice conflict objects store both sides plus base as content-addressed blob references, not as an algebraic patch type; a checkpoint containing conflicts is legal, syncable and publishable; resolution is a later checkpoint naming the conflict object it resolves.
Un-conflicting is implemented as `ltx undo` on the operation that introduced the side — an op-log pointer move, not an inverse-merge computation.

Every file and directory entry in the Merkle tree carries an intrinsic entry_id distinct from its path (Pijul's name-vertex/inode-vertex split), so rename-vs-edit and rename-vs-rename are distinguishable at merge time.

Deletion records the change that introduced the deleted content (required G2.1 scenario), and ADR-1 must either budget for the per-range attribution index this requires in a snapshot model or explicitly scope the guarantee to whole-entry deletions in v1.

Gate G3.2: an audit assertion that no XOR or additive accumulator appears in any LTX-SYNC set summary, plus an adversarial test that attempts to construct a colliding set digest under the chosen scheme and must fail — scoped to the places sync negotiation digests a genuinely unordered set (e.g. 'the set of checkpoint IDs I hold'), since ordered Merkle trees are already safe.

Record the tree-sitter grammar identity and version used for each structural merge in the resulting checkpoint's provenance, and surface semantic-layer fallback in `ltx internals` even when quiet in normal output.
Gate `ltx record` and `ltx sync` on p99.9 latency rather than mean.

Conflict display carries the provenance of both sides (checkpoint, actor, change) as a first-class element, not behind `ltx internals`; propose a gate measuring whether a user can identify the origin of a conflict, since none exists today.

uncomfortable_findings: entry_id cannot survive a Git round trip. Git trees carry no file identity — renames are inferred heuristically at read time — so an entry_id minted in Lattice is dropped on export and unrecoverable on re-import. Every `ltx sync` through a plain-Git teammate silently degrades the exact identity mechanism (Pijul's name-vertex/inode-vertex split) that makes rename-vs-edit and rename-vs-rename resolvable. The correspondence table must carry path ↔ entry_id per exported commit, keyed by lens version, or the mechanism fails precisely for the teams the bridge exists to serve.

Per-change deletion provenance has an unpriced cost in a snapshot model. Pijul gets it free because every edge already carries its introducing change. Lattice would need a per-range attribution index over live content, maintained incrementally — that is a blame index, precisely the structure snapshot systems are bad at. Either budget for it in ADR-1 or scope the parallel-delete-then-one-revert guarantee to whole-entry deletions in v1.

Making conflicts first-class values does not make them correct. Darcs' conflictors — the direct ancestor of Lattice's conflict objects — carried documented soundness bugs for over a decade: the Darcs wiki says the tracking of a conflictor's three components under commutation 'apparently has bugs', and issue2047 records that commuting a conflictor with a duplicate is not guaranteed invertible. Lattice's simpler blob-reference carrier avoids the algebra but inherits the obligation to prove the resolution semantics.

The prior draft's central Mimram & Di Giusto claim was technically wrong in a way that matters. The free cocompletion's objects are finite sets labelled by lines with a TRANSITIVE RELATION, and the paper explicitly says 'we have to allow cycles'. A partial order is antisymmetric and cannot represent cyclic conflicts — including the directory-rename cycle Pijul catalogues. Any Lattice conflict model built as 'a partial order over identified lines' is provably too weak for a conflict class the prior art already enumerated.

Darcs' merge-complexity argument does not transplant to Lattice's model, and the derived gate was mis-parameterised. Darcs' exponential blowup was in the number of patches involved; Lattice's three-way merge is bounded by the size of the two sides, not by history depth. Demanding 'sub-quadratic in conflicting-change count' is stricter than the evidence (darcs-3 achieved quadratic and judged it testable) and measures a parameter Lattice's merge does not have. The transplantable constraint is the CI wall-clock budget that made 10^5 fuzz cases possible at all.

Commutativity of merge cannot be asserted on merged tree bytes. A three-way merge that emits conflict regions is legitimately side-ordered, so merge(a,b) == merge(b,a) on raw bytes either fails on correct output or forces an arbitrary canonical side-order into the on-disk format. The assertion has to be made over a normal form that treats the conflict's two sides as an unordered set — which is a format constraint on conflict objects, not just a test detail.

Pijul's Git round-trip has been an open problem since January 2022 and has not shipped. Meunier's obstacle is model-level, not effort-level: commits cannot be produced from patches independently of the other applied patches, so a re-imported commit can be duplicated under a new hash and generate 'lots of unintelligible conflicts'. Lattice's snapshot choice makes the bridge tractable but not solved, and lens-defined export makes it HARDER than a naive 1:1 export because the mapping is many-to-one and lens definitions change between syncs. This is the single highest-risk subsystem in the spec.

Darcs shipped `darcs rebase` in 2.10.0 (19 April 2015) despite already having order-independent cherry-pick, explicitly 'to enable deep amending of history' — and its own performance FAQ then recommends rebase as a way to avoid exponential merges. Lattice's claim that lenses replace rebase is over-claimed: lenses are read-path projections and cannot amend, split, or drop the dependencies of a recorded change.

Pijul's 1.0-beta post concedes that patch-based VCS have always traded intuitive patches against navigable snapshots, and introduces tags — compressed repository snapshots — specifically to make browsing a past state efficient. Any Lattice feature that tries to present history purely as a set of changes hits the same wall.

Pijul's own FAQ (2020–2023) answered 'Do files merged by Pijul always have the correct semantic?' with 'No.' A provably sound pushout-based merge does not deliver semantic correctness. Lattice's tree-sitter structural merge — a heuristic over a regenerable, possibly stale index — claims more than Pijul does with a stronger foundation, and can be WORSE than line merge when the parse is partial or the grammar mismatched. (That FAQ entry has since been quietly removed from the live site, which is itself a signal about how the claim aged.)

'Degrades silently to line/byte behaviour' makes merge non-deterministic across clients: two developers with different tree-sitter grammar versions produce different merge results from identical inputs, invisibly. Silent and reproducible are in direct tension, and silent degradation breaks the determinism assertions every G2.1 property depends on.

Pijul's own beta benchmarks show pathological tails on ordinary repositories despite a sound model: one Vim commit took 5m16s to import (of 15,138); one Ruby commit ~25s to record and ~408s to apply (of 70,859); 913 of 52,664 CPython commits (1.7%) exceeded 5s to record; and one no-op commit cost 48.7s because Pijul re-diffed all 3,706 files. That last case is the exact shape a continuous auto-snapshotter with CDC on all content will hit, and worst cases — not averages — drive abandonment.

Convergence and accurate conflict modelling are separate properties, and Lattice's carrier only buys the first. Pijul states it would remain a CRDT with or without per-change edge labels — the labels exist solely so conflicts are modelled ACCURATELY. Lattice's blob-reference conflict objects get convergence cheaply; the accuracy property must be earned separately by G2.1, and cannot be assumed from the fact that conflicts are stored rather than blocked.

Darcs had a SMALLER conceptual surface than Git and still lost on UX. GHC's specific complaint was diagnostic, not conceptual: in a conflict you could not tell which two patches were conflicting. Lattice's 'seven user-facing nouns' target measures conceptual economy, which is a different property from diagnosability, and the spec currently gates neither.

Adoption evidence challenges theoretical superiority as a differentiator: after ten years Pijul draws 1,877 crate downloads a quarter while Jujutsu — snapshot-based, Git-backed by default, first published on crates.io seven years later — draws 25,621, roughly 13.6x. (Caveat the earlier draft omitted: gix's 9.6M is a library-dependency count, not users, and cargo undercounts jj, which ships via Homebrew and nix — so the direction is robust, the multiple is not.) Nothing in Lattice's agent-provenance differentiator obviously moves that number more than Git compatibility does.

Sittampalam's 2005 note is weaker support for stable change IDs than the earlier draft claimed. Footnote 4 hedges — 'I think it would require some kind of stronger property, such as unique patch ids' — offering unique ids as an example, not the identified answer, in an informal working document whose own footnotes read 'This is horrible. I need a better notation.' Lattice must not assume its stable change IDs deliver the identity properties it wants; that is exactly what G2.1 has to measure.

Formal foundations lengthen timelines rather than shortening them. Eighteen years passed from the June 2002 Darcs design to the first implementation without exponential merge (darcs-3, August 2020), and as of the darcs 2.18.5 man page it is still marked EXPERIMENTAL, a technology preview, 'we do NOT recommend to use it for any serious work', with darcs-2 remaining the default — twenty-four years without a default-on sound implementation. Pijul's own 2020 FAQ made the point: 'categories are neither algorithms nor data structures in themselves.'

The strongest incumbency signal in this prior art is not that Darcs lost — it is how slowly it lost. GHC's maintainers documented catastrophic, quantified failures in 2008 and voted that a change would be beneficial, and the project still did not move until March 2011; at ICFP'10 the community was 'roughly a 50/50 split' with 'no immediate plans to switch'. Measured defects in the incumbent do not produce migration. Lattice's adoption model should assume switching costs dominate evidence.

title: Fossil
q3_concrete_actions: ADR-REDACT-01 / `Tombstone` struct: the tombstone is a first-class op-log entry in GLOBAL (syncable) state with exactly these fields — redacted content hash, pre-image chunk-tree root, redactor Ed25519 public key, timestamp, reason code from a CLOSED enum, and an Ed25519 signature over all of the above. Contrast: Fossil's `shun(uuid, mtime, scom)` sits below the global/local divider at schema.c line 155, is unsigned, has no actor, and its reason is free text.

ADR-REDACT-01 / Merkle encoding: the redacted child slot in the parent directory tree is replaced by `H(tombstone)`, never emptied, so the enclosing directory-tree root still verifies after redaction.

Gate G-VERIFY-OFFLINE, blocking on `ltx verify`: a peer that has NEVER held the plaintext must verify a redacted checkpoint's Merkle root and enumerate who authorised each removal with no network access. Test fixture: clone into a fresh store, assert `ltx verify --offline` exits 0 and `ltx trace --redactions` names the redactor key for every tombstone.

Redaction path: implement Fossil's `content_undelta`-before-delete invariant (src/shun.c `shun_artifacts()`) at chunk level — before deleting a redacted chunk, re-materialize every non-redacted chunk-tree that references it.

Constraint on ADR-STORE-01 (store-backend benchmark): the backend MUST maintain a persistent `chunk_hash -> referencing_chunk_tree` reverse index, and the redaction path MUST issue a pre-flight fan-out query against it. The benchmark MUST measure reverse-index maintenance cost on write, not only read throughput — otherwise it selects a backend (custom append-only packs) that cannot ship chunk-level redaction without an O(repository) scan.

ADR-PROV-01: provenance is a signed field of the checkpoint artifact in global state; only the query index is derived. Contrast: Fossil's `rcvfrom(rcvid, uid, mtime, nonce, ipaddr)` is at schema.c line 104, below the divider, and blockchain.md confirms the rcvfrom table has size 1 after clone.

Gate G-PROV-REBUILD: clone to a peer that has never seen the repo, delete the provenance index, run `ltx internals reindex`, and require `ltx trace --agent --unreviewed --touching src/auth/` to return byte-identical output to the origin.

ADR-PROV-01 amendment (NEW, forced by the Fossil `scrub` precedent): split provenance into a signed actor-KEY field (global, pseudonymous, never erasable) and a key->human-identity BINDING held in local/side state that `ltx scrub` can erase. Without the split, 'provenance is global and signed' and 'GDPR identity erasure is affordable' cannot both hold, because erasing an identity would require a tombstone against every checkpoint that actor authored.

ADR-REDACT-01 sync path: a tombstone arriving from a remote is QUARANTINED — it suppresses serving the content and marks it redacted-pending, but does not destroy local bytes until an actor holding a key in the repo's local `trusted_redactors` set countersigns. No setting may make acceptance automatic; this is a design constraint, not a default. Direct inverse of `SETTING: auto-shun boolean default=on` (src/db.c line 4681).
Op-log schema: `TombstoneReceived` and `TombstoneAccepted` are two distinct operation kinds, so `ltx undo` reverses the local acceptance while the received tombstone remains on the record.

Op-log schema + Gate G-UNDO-TOTAL: every op-log entry for a mutation of NON-content repository state (settings, remote config, lens definitions, key material, review attestations) must record a pre-image hash of the affected state. The gate is a property test: for every variant of the `Operation` enum, apply it to a fixture repo, run `ltx undo`, and assert the full repository state hash returns to its pre-operation value. Any operation kind without an inverse fails the build.

Attestation ordering rule (NEW): review attestations are ordered by op-log position (Merkle-linked, tamper-evident), NEVER by a wall-clock timestamp field. Fossil's fileformat.wiki resolves competing tags by 'the tag with the latest (most recent) date', where the date is the artifact's own self-asserted D card — an actor changes a review status by claiming a later date.

ADR-BRIDGE-01: store the lens-output-to-checkpoint correspondence durably inside the repository as op-log entries, not an out-of-band sidecar (Fossil's `.mirror_state`, which users are told 'Do not put those files under Git management. Do not edit or delete them.').

ADR-BRIDGE-01: pin one lens version per Git remote in a `LensPin{remote, lens_id, lens_version}` record. Changing a pinned lens is a first-class signed logged operation kind (`LensRepin`) whose CLI output declares 'this rewrites published Git history for remote X'. `ltx sync` MUST refuse to push a shape change under an unchanged pin.

Proposed gate G-NOUN-BUDGET: a CI check that fails if any noun outside the allowlist of seven appears in user-facing help text — Fossil started at four nouns and shipped 120 commands and 116 settings, and its `test-*` split (157 commands) did not stop porcelain growth.

Schema-boundary practice: place the global/local (syncable/derived) divider physically inside the store's schema source module, as Fossil does at schema.c lines 94-98, and gate it in CI — not only in the design document.
uncomfortable_findings: ADR-PROV-01 AND ADR-REDACT-01 ARE IN DIRECT CONFLICT, and no draft acknowledged it. Fossil can honour a GDPR identity-erasure request cheaply precisely BECAUSE provenance is local state: `fossil scrub --verily` deletes 'concealed email addresses, IP addresses of correspondents, and similar privacy-sensitive fields' while shunning.wiki confirms 'in the DAG, commits by bertina will continue to be visible unchanged.' Lattice's headline commitment — move provenance INTO the signed global artifact — destroys that cheap path. Erasing one actor's identity then requires a signed tombstone against every checkpoint they ever authored. 'Provenance is global and signed' and 'GDPR erasure is affordable' cannot both hold unless the ADR splits pseudonymous actor-key (global) from key-to-identity binding (local, scrubbable).

REVIEW ATTESTATIONS ORDERED BY TIMESTAMP ARE FORGEABLE, and Fossil already has the bug. fileformat.wiki: 'When two or more tags with the same name are applied to the same artifact, the tag with the latest (most recent) date is used' — where the date is the artifact's own self-asserted D card. Lattice's 'review status updatable by later attestation without rewriting checkpoints' inherits this exactly: an agent or human upgrades its own review status by claiming a later timestamp. Signatures do not help; the signature covers the lie. Ordering must come from op-log position, not a clock field.

STRUCTURAL VERIFICATION IS NOT SEMANTIC SURVIVAL. H(tombstone) preserves the Merkle root, which is the whole of Lattice's stated redaction win — but Fossil maintainer Stephan Beal states the残 real cost: shunning 'breaks it when it removes records which are referenced by other records. e.g., shunning a file semantically breaks any commit which refers to it and any commits which derive from those commits.' Lattice has no defined degraded-read behaviour for a checkpoint containing a tombstone — what `ltx diff`, structural merge, and the tree-sitter index do — so the spec currently promises a verifiable tree that no command can usefully read.

APPEND-ONLY STORAGE DOES NOT BUY YOU UNDO. Fossil has had immutable storage for 19 years and its undo is weaker than Git's reflog: 'A single level of undo/redo is supported. The undo/redo stack is cleared by the commit and check-out commands.' It covers exactly eight commands (update, merge, revert, stash pop/apply/drop/goto, clean), `fossil clean` 'only saves state for files less than 10MiB in size', and the stack lives in the checkout DB. The hard part of universal undo is not the content store — it is operations touching non-content-addressed state (settings, remotes, lens definitions, keys, attestations). `ltx undo` covers 'everything' only over the content-addressed subset unless every Operation variant records a pre-image hash.

REDACTION UNDER GLOBAL CDC IS FAR MORE EXPENSIVE THAN UNDER FOSSIL'S MODEL, AND POSSIBLY UNBOUNDED. Fossil's `delta(rid, srcid)` fan-out is essentially one version chain per path, so `content_undelta` touches a handful of artifacts. Lattice's chunk-level dedup means one chunk may be referenced by an unbounded number of chunk-trees across unrelated files — redacting a common boilerplate chunk (licence header, import block) could force re-materialization of gigabytes. Cost scales with reference fan-out, not with the size of the file the user asked to redact. Fossil avoided this only by not deduplicating below file granularity.

LOCAL WRITE ACCESS DEFEATS EVERY IMMUTABILITY GUARANTEE, and Fossil says so in fossil-v-git.wiki (NOT shunning.wiki, where this is usually mis-cited): 'if shunning and purging were removed from Fossil, you could still remove artifacts from the repository with SQL DELETE statements; the repository database file is, after all, directly modifiable, being writable by your user.' `.lattice/` is likewise owner-writable. Signed tombstones prove a redaction HAPPENED; nothing proves a silent deletion did NOT. The defensible guarantee is 'no checkpointed data is silently lost across an honest sync', not 'no data loss'.

DOCUMENTATION AND DEFAULTS CAN DISAGREE ABOUT THE MOST DESTRUCTIVE FEATURE, AND IN FOSSIL THEY DO. shunning.wiki makes an absolute claim: 'By refusing to propagate the shunning list, Fossil ensures that no remote user will ever be able to remove information from your personal repositories without your permission.' src/db.c line 4681 ships `SETTING: auto-shun boolean default=on` — 'automatically pull the shunning list from a server to which the client autosyncs' — and tech_overview.wiki adds 'The shun table is also copied during a clone.' Forum (Andy Bradford): the server 'will also publish the shunned artifacts list to clients and they will remove it from their repositories automatically.' The docs describe the Admin-gated UPWARD direction and over-generalise it. Lattice's tombstone propagation carries the identical hazard: a compromised remote gains power to destroy content on every peer.

THE GIT BRIDGE TARGET IS VERY LIKELY UNREALISTIC, AND IT SHIPS FIRST. mirrortogithub.md: 'The mirroring is one-way... There are technical problems that make a two-way mirror all but impossible', therefore 'you cannot accept pull requests on GitHub.' `fossil git import MIRROR`'s built-in help still reads literally 'TBD...' at trunk tip 2.29 (2026-08-28) — verified today, seven years after the mirror shipped in 2.9. A simpler model built by an exceptionally capable engineer over 19 years did not achieve what Lattice specifies as a CORE subsystem shipping BEFORE the semantic and agent layers.

THREE LATTICE CLAIMS ARE MUTUALLY INCONSISTENT: (a) `ltx sync` speaks to Git remotes so plain-Git teammates notice nothing; (b) Lattice-to-Git published history is LENS-DEFINED; (c) no force-push concept exists. A lens is a non-injective projection and lenses are versioned — when a pinned lens version changes, the generated Git commit graph changes shape and updating the remote is a non-fast-forward update, i.e. a force-push against a remote plain-Git teammates are pulling from. Denying the concept removes the warning, not the operation.

BUNDLING IS WHAT MADE FOSSIL'S GIT INTEROP IRREVERSIBLY ONE-WAY, because the bundled objects (wiki, tickets, forum, unversioned files, non-unique tags) have no Git representation — and the mapping had to be materialised in an out-of-band `.mirror_state` directory because it is not derivable from content. This validates Lattice's non-goals but implies that ANY Lattice object without a Git analogue (provenance signatures, conflict objects, changesets, lens definitions, op-log entries) is a candidate for the same lossiness. Lattice's agent-native layer is precisely such an object, so 'plain-Git teammates notice nothing' means 'the differentiator is invisible across the bridge'.

SINGLE-HASH CONTENT ADDRESSING HAS A COMMON-MODE FAILURE FOSSIL DELIBERATELY ENGINEERS AROUND. selfcheck.wiki: the R-card and Z-card 'use a different hash algorithm (MD5) in order to avoid common-mode failures in the hash algorithm implementation', plus a 32-bit checksum in the delta format and a re-extract-and-verify pass before every transaction commit, accepted at 'a substantial performance cost' because 'reliability is more important than raw speed'. Lattice's BLAKE3-only design has no independent detector: a hash-implementation bug cannot be caught by the thing it corrupts.

THE SEVEN-NOUN BUDGET IS NOT DEFENDED BY INTENT. Fossil started from a four-noun model and, counted from its live help index on 2026-09-03, ships 120 commands, 116 settings and 226 web pages plus 157 'Unsupported and Testing Commands'. NOTE — the draft's supporting comparison was wrong and is now corrected: Git 2.50.1 reports 170 commands via `git --list-cmds=main` (144 builtins), so Fossil's porcelain is SMALLER than Git's, not larger. The finding survives the correction and is sharper for it: the failure is not that Fossil exceeded Git, it is that a four-noun conceptual model produced 120 commands and a 116-setting configuration surface anyway, and Fossil's `test-*` escape hatch (structurally identical to `ltx internals`) did not stop porcelain growth.

DIVERGENCE HAS NO GUARANTEED CONVERGENCE. blockchain.md: Fossil is 'an AP-mode system, which means there can be no guaranteed consensus on the content of the ledger at any given time' and 'you cannot guarantee that the command fossil info tip gives the same result everywhere.' Lattice's peer-to-peer sync with no force-push inherits this exactly: a signed retraction is itself just another artifact peers may or may not have pulled. 'Converges by merge or a logged signed retraction' is an eventual-consistency claim, not a guarantee.

ROADMAP ORDERING IS SELF-DEFEATING. The spec ships the Git bridge BEFORE lenses. If the bridge fixes published-history shape in v0, lenses inherit that shape as a compatibility constraint, and 'lens-defined export' is retrofitted onto a shape chosen before the lens system existed.

title: Sapling (Meta)
q3_concrete_actions: G1.3: every ltx-oplog operation record carries a `pre` field of three root hashes (autosnapshot root, checkpoint-DAG root, ref-set root); over 100,000 generated operation sequences from the full verb set, `ltx undo` after every prefix restores a state whose recomputed roots equal the recorded `pre` triple, with zero patch applications on the undo path. Explicitly framed as PARITY with jj, not differentiation.
G1.3 (second clause): `ltx undo` must never refuse to run because working state is dirty — the inverse of Sapling's `cmdutil.bailifchanged(repo)`, which guards three call sites in undo.py.

G1.4: no code path in the ltx-oplog undo subsystem may reference the CLI argument parser; enforced by a crate-level lint denying `ltx-cli` parser symbols from `ltx-oplog`. Undo/redo navigate the Merkle-linked op-log DAG by parent pointer using structured arguments (contrast: Sapling's `sl redo` re-parses recorded argv via `cliparser.parsecommand`).

G1.5: the `ltx-store` mutation API is private and reachable only through an `ltx-oplog::OpTransaction` handle, so no repo mutation can commit without its operation record; verified by crash-injection tests (kill at N points across the write path) asserting zero orphan mutations. A store mutation with no op-log record is a hard failure, not a gap marker (contrast: Sapling's `safelog` swallows a 2-second `undolog/lock` timeout and proceeds unlogged, writing a `gap` sentinel).

G1.6: op-log thinning exists; each thinning event is itself an appended operation record; thinning may never remove a record that is the `pre`-image of a reachable checkpoint; corruption recovery is per-record (quarantine and skip), never whole-log deletion (contrast: Sapling's `_nukerevlogs` calls `localvfs.rmtree("undolog")` on a revlog/mpatch error, destroying all undo history).

G2.1: benchmark Lattice FastCDC-over-all-content + zstd against fixed-size chunking + zstd dictionary/delta compression (the Mononoke `FilestoreParams{chunk_size, concurrency}` + Packblob baseline), on a corpus of large binaries mutated by head-insertion; require >=2x reduction in stored bytes. Delta compression must be held CONSTANT across both arms — comparing CDC to fixed chunking without delta compression guarantees a win and proves nothing. On failure, the all-content-CDC decision reverts to CDC above a size threshold with whole-file addressing below it.

ADR-014: constrains `ltx assign` to absorb's two invariants — no 3-way merge (line-provenance assignment only, so it cannot conflict) and it never writes to working state; ambiguous changes are left in working state untouched and reported. q3_concrete_actions: Gate G2.1 (hash independence): checkpoint Merkle roots are computed from BLAKE3 chunk trees over bytes only; the semantic index under .lattice/index/ is never an input to any hash. Over a corpus of >=1,000 repositories, delete and rebuild the index and assert every checkpoint root hash is byte-identical; a single mismatch fails the gate.

Entity IDs live in a sidecar binding table mapping (checkpoint_id, path, byte_range) -> entity_id with confidence: f32 and origin enum {heuristic, confirmed, inherited}, stored outside the Merkle root so an index rebuild can revise a heuristic binding without rewriting history.

When no tree-sitter grammar covers a file, or the parse yields ERROR nodes over the changed range, entity granularity falls back to file-level and the binding is tagged origin=heuristic, confidence=0.

Gate G2.4 (loud degradation, NEW): ltx trace emits a coverage: line in every result set (e.g. 'semantic coverage: 71% of touched bytes; 4 files line-only'); G2.4 asserts the line is present and numerically correct on a fixture set containing at least one file with no grammar and at least one file whose parse yields ERROR nodes.

Rename and cross-file-move confirmations are recorded as entity.bind operations in the append-only Merkle-linked op-log, Ed25519-signed with the same provenance record as a checkpoint (actor class, identity, tool/model/version), making them durable, syncable, auditable and covered by ltx undo.
The heuristic matcher treats confirmations as hard constraints: it may fill gaps but may never contradict a confirmation, and must never overwrite one on index rebuild.

Do not build a second, name-aware hash to distinguish human edits from machine-propagated ones; the provenance layer's actor class already records this as primary data on every checkpoint. Record the trade in an ADR, because the temptation recurs at every merge (Unison invented the syntactic hash nine years in).

Gate G2.2: measure and publish recall and precision of entity continuation on a hand-labelled corpus of >=500 real rename/move commits across >=6 languages, exposed via ltx internals index stats, with a stated floor below which ltx trace refuses to report entity-level results.

Gate G2.3: assert incremental-vs-fresh index equivalence over a generated edit-sequence corpus, since tree-sitter incremental parses can differ from fresh parses of the same file and the defect lives in grammars Lattice does not own.

Adopt Unison's monotone refactoring-frontier framing for changesets and conflict objects, but produce the worklist by topological sort over a graph whose cycles are SCC-collapsed and surfaced as a unit, with a property test asserting no ordering ever revisits a node -- because Unison's shipped todo ordering 'sometimes leads you in a circle'.
Borrow the v2 LocalIds technique in the chunk store: serialized objects carry a local-to-global id lookup table so ltx sync rewrites only the table, never the blob body.

ADR on agent key custody (SHARPENED): decide who may hold an agent-class Ed25519 key, whether an agent-signed entity.bind is a confirmation or only a high-confidence heuristic, and what ltx trace --agent reports when a signature attests only to key possession rather than to actor class.

The most committed append-only, immutable, content-addressed, Merkle-causal design in existence still needed the escape hatch and named it. Lattice's 'no force-push concept exists' is a stronger claim than the closest prior art could sustain, and needs an ADR saying what Lattice's equivalent override is rather than asserting none is required.

Lens-defined Lattice->Git published history IS a force-push from the Git side. If generated Git commit hashes are a function of the lens, changing a lens rewrites published Git history. Unison's trajectory is the warning: its v1 format was deliberately built to ride Git (file-per-hash directories, `dependents/` shaped so 'git merge of dependents does the right thing') and was abandoned for SQLite and then a from-scratch Share host, because the foreign host could not render its model. Requires per-ref lens pinning and refusal to re-export under a changed lens without a logged operation.

Structural hashing is not solved even when you own the entire language. Unison issue #2787 (opened 2022-01-06, still open) shows term NAMES leaking into the cycle hash for mutually recursive definitions: canonical ordering ignores self-referential variables, ties fall through to alphabetical name order, so equivalent cycles can get different hashes and different cycles could collide. The shipped mitigation, PR #6007 (merged 2025-12-04, nine days after 1.0.0, released in 1.0.1), does not fix it -- it makes hashing crash via `error`, and the author writes this is 'the first introduction of the idea that hashing a component could fail; which is undesirable.' The workaround is inserting an inert dummy binding.

Unison's own version control had to reintroduce NAMES into a hash to work. PR #4910 (merged 2024-05-16) diffs namespaces by 'syntactic hashes' in which a pretty-print environment renders references before hashing -- explicitly 'the mechanism by which we distinguish user changes from auto-propagated changes.' PR #5716 does rename detection by syntactic hash, not content hash. Nine years in, pure content addressing was insufficient for VCS operations. Any Lattice claim that structural identity alone solves rename/move tracking is contradicted by the most committed implementation of the idea.

Provenance is a key-custody problem that nobody has solved, and Lattice's spec does not address it. Unison ships an MCP server with 29 tools, 8 flagged destructiveHint=true, including update, rename, move, delete, delete.namespace and CreateBranchTool (added in 1.1.1 explicitly 'to allow AI to create branches'). Its operation log, `project_branch_reflog`, has columns project_id, project_branch_id, time, from_root_causal_id, to_root_causal_id, reason -- and NO actor column; authorship exists only as `create.author`, an ordinary unsigned Author definition hand-attached as metadata. The space is genuinely unoccupied, which validates Lattice's differentiator, but when an agent shells out to `ltx` it holds whatever key is on the machine, usually the human's, so an Ed25519 signature attests to key possession, not actor class.

Heuristic entity matching will be materially worse than the tools Lattice will be compared against, and the gap is infrastructural. RefactoringMiner's live accuracy page reports 0.999 precision / 0.984 recall on a 547-commit Java oracle, plus Python (0.996/0.997, 202 commits), Kotlin (0.998/1.000, 63 commits) and JavaScript (0.978/1.000, 25 commits) -- so 'Java only' is false. But those numbers rest on Eclipse JDT, kotlin-compiler-embeddable, Eclipse CDT and SWC/swc4j; its tree-sitter path is a GumTree gen.treesitter-ng BETA, and its own roadmap leaves 'Validate precision/recall' unchecked for Kotlin and JavaScript. tree-sitter yields a concrete syntax tree with no binding resolution. Git's rename detection defaults to 50% similarity and gives up past 1,000 files. A silent false negative in `ltx trace --agent --unreviewed --touching src/auth/` is worse than no feature.

tree-sitter is not deterministic across edit paths, and the defect lives in grammars Lattice does not own and cannot get fixed. Issue #4001 documents an incremental parse producing an ERROR node where a fresh parse of the identical file does not; maintainers closed it 'not planned', and the reporter himself could not tell whether the fault was in tree-sitter core or in tree-sitter-haskell -- whose issue #129 has been open since 2024-09-22 with ZERO comments. Grammar coverage also decays: tree-sitter-toml and tree-sitter-swift are ARCHIVED in the official org, and Cargo.toml is in every Rust repo.

A queryable derived index becomes de facto authoritative regardless of what the bytes say, and this collides head-on with redaction. Unison's syntactic hash started as an internal merge helper and now DEFINES what a rename is. Once `ltx trace --agent --unreviewed` is used for compliance sign-off, its output IS the record for that purpose. A signed tombstone destroys the bytes the index was built from, so a post-redaction rebuild yields different entity bindings than the pre-redaction index and two audits of the same history disagree.

'Seven user-facing nouns, total' is not a complexity bound, and the measured counterexample is decisive. UCM's `help` lists 119 primary commands plus 67 aliases -- 186 invocable names -- over roughly six nouns, with four separate reflog commands accreted around one concept, and `patch` deleted outright rather than kept. Conceptual load lives in verb semantics. Replace the noun count with a CI-enforced verb budget.

Universal undo is unproven. UCM's `undo` 'reverts the most recent change to the codebase' -- single-step. Lattice promises undo of everything including merges, syncs and undo itself. Nothing in the closest prior art demonstrates that composability, and undo-of-undo interacts with the op-log, lens composition and sync in ways no shipped system has validated.

The monotone refactoring frontier is a design-document property, not a shipped one. The covering/escaped-dependent metric 'will decrease monotonically' appears in a historical design document; the shipped `todo` does print 'I recommend working on them in the following order', but Unison's own update-process post lists among the old workflow's defects that 'the suggested order of edits sometimes leads you in a circle.' Lattice must not assume an acyclic worklist falls out of a monotone metric.

The scale evidence argues against front-loading the semantic layer. Unison took ten and a half years to 1.0 (repo 2015-05-06; 1.0.0 2025-11-25) and today has 6,720 stars, 308 forks, 1,219 open issues plus 49 open PRs, and 118 unique projects in its curated Share catalog -- while OWNING the language, typechecker and runtime. Lattice's semantic problem is strictly harder (N languages, no ownership, no typechecker, grammars that get archived) and is scheduled third behind the Git bridge. Structural merge and cross-file entity identity should be labelled v2 in the roadmap now.

title: SemanticMerge, difftastic and GumTree
q3_concrete_actions: G4 entity-match gate is split into three separately-gated tiers: G4-A (type/class/module/enum) at >=99% precision / >=95% recall; G4-B (functions/methods) at >=95% precision / >=75% recall, conditional on ADR-SM-01 shipping and reported alongside an un-anchored baseline; G4-C (fields/variables/statements) measured and reported in the G4 artifact but NOT gated in v1.

ADR-SM-01: LTX's matcher performs signature-scoped anchoring (match declarations by signature first, then match the remainder by signature plus body) before general tree matching — the IJM mechanism, which is what lifts method precision from 93.5% to 99.4% and overall precision to 99.6% in the Alikhanifard/Tsantalis benchmark.

ADR-SM-02 (structural-merge acceptance rule): a structural resolution is written as merged bytes only if (a) line merge also produces a clean result and the two byte sequences agree, or (b) the disagreement is confined to a commutative parent declared for that language in languages.toml; otherwise LTX emits a conflict object. Adapted from — not identical to — S3M's per-handler use of unstructured merge as an oracle.

Structural merge is a proposal recorded as an attestation on the first-class conflict object, never a rewrite of bytes; acceptance is a later checkpoint and `ltx undo` reverses acceptance as an op-log pointer move.

G4's silent mis-merge metric is redefined as: of conflict objects the structural merger proposed to auto-resolve, the fraction whose proposed bytes differ from the resolution checkpoint that actually landed in the op-log.
The op-log mis-merge metric is explicitly classified as post-release retrospective telemetry, NOT a pre-release gate; G4 at v1 ships against a fixed corpus, because at v1 no user history exists.
The op-log mis-merge rate is recorded as a lower bound on true error, because the developer sees the proposal before resolving; an unbiased number requires a withheld-proposal control cohort.

Ship named limit constants LTX_SEMANTIC_BYTE_LIMIT (seed 1,000,000), LTX_SEMANTIC_NODE_LIMIT (seed 3,000,000) and LTX_PARSE_ERROR_LIMIT (seed 0), explicitly marked provisional and requiring re-benchmarking against LTX's own GumTree-family matcher rather than inheriting difftastic's Dijkstra-calibrated values.

Count work actually performed rather than estimating it in advance when applying the node limit, and apply the limit per changed region rather than per file — following difftastic's --node-limit to --graph-limit migration and its per-section application in src/main.rs.

ADR-SM-03: every semantic-layer fallback is written to the op-log as a `semantic_fallback` operation carrying a reason enum (byte limit / node limit / parse error / no grammar), queryable via `ltx trace --semantic-fallback`; this inverts the spec's 'degrades silently' decision for the record while staying silent in the UI.

ADR-SM-04: Lattice defines no grammar format of its own and binds to upstream tree-sitter grammars; the derived semantic index is keyed on (grammar name, grammar content hash, matcher parameter set) so a grammar upgrade invalidates and regenerates rather than silently changing merge behaviour.

ADR-SM-05: a checkpoint recording a structural resolution carries the grammar content hash and matcher parameter set in its Ed25519-signed provenance, and native sync ships an explicit peer-convergence-under-grammar-skew test.

Ship a machine-readable languages.toml support manifest with a coverage tier per language (per-language commutative-parent sets, signature definitions, isomorphism rules) and evaluate G4 per tier per language, never as a single repo-wide average.

ADR-SM-06 (merge pipeline order): line merge first; on conflict, reconstruct fictional revisions from the conflicted line-merge output and seed the structural pass with matchings already established; whole-file structural only if conflicts persist.

ADR-SM-07: merged artifacts are always reassembled from byte spans and never printed from the syntax tree, and the semantic index must tile every character of a file with no gaps (SemanticMerge's no-holes invariant).
Universal undo replays the recorded proposal bytes rather than regenerating a proposal, so that undo/redo remains an involution across a grammar upgrade.
Entity-scoped `ltx trace` queries are restricted to Tier A entities or must report their own recall, so the agent-provenance headline feature does not silently under-report.
Gate conflict reduction and silent mis-merge rate as a Pareto pair in G4 rather than as two independent thresholds.
uncomfortable_findings: ADR-SM-02 is either safe-and-useless or entirely dependent on per-language handwork. Clause (a) writes structural bytes only when line merge is already clean and byte-identical — exactly the case where structural merge contributes nothing. All value collapses into clause (b), the commutative-parent carve-out, which is the same hand-written per-language configuration Mergiraf demonstrates does not generalise. The >=20% conflict-reduction target may be unreachable BECAUSE of the safety rule.

First-class conflict objects relocate the auto-resolve-vs-block trade-off rather than removing it, contrary to the claim that Lattice's design dissolves it. Something must still decide whether the working tree materialises the proposal: materialise by default and silent mis-merge exposure equals any other tool; do not materialise and conflict reduction cannot be claimed. Pareto-pairing the G4 metrics names the trade-off without resolving it.

The op-log ground-truth oracle is anchored by the very proposal it scores. If LTX shows a developer a proposed structural resolution and they accept it, the 'resolution that actually landed' IS the proposal, so the metric measures agreement with the tool's own suggestion, not correctness. The measured mis-merge rate is a lower bound; an unbiased estimate requires a withheld-proposal control arm.

The op-log oracle cannot be a pre-release gate. OOPSLA'17 states the merged-code oracle 'is only available after the merge result has been committed. So a handler could not rely on that.' At v1 Lattice has no user history, so G4 must be evaluated against a fixed corpus and the op-log metric is post-release telemetry. Conflating the two would make G4 unevaluable at ship time.

G4's >=99% entity-match precision is achievable by a generic GumTree-family matcher, contradicting the claim that only Java-only RefactoringMiner reaches it — IJM scores 99.4% precision on methods and 99.6% overall via signature-scoped partial matching. This is good news that carries a cost: it means the >=99% target is defensible only if Lattice actually builds signature anchoring, and the number is still measured on Eclipse JDT ASTs, not a tree-sitter CST.

G4's recall target fails badly on fields regardless of matcher choice: best published field recall across all six benchmarked tools is 59.2%, GumTree 3.0 greedy is 52.2%, and IJM — the precision winner — is the WORST at 44.5%. Field/variable matching cannot be gated in v1 by any published technique.

All entity-match precision/recall figures are computed only over program elements whose AST subtree actually changed; identical subtrees were excluded because every tool matches them at 100%. Only 4.8% of method declarations and 1.5% of field declarations changed in the benchmark. Any claim of '~20% under-reporting for methods, ~48% for fields' as a repo-wide figure is wrong by roughly an order of magnitude — though errors compound across long histories.

Tier A's >=95% recall target is imported from a number Lattice's own architecture undercuts. The 98.7% figure for type declarations comes from Eclipse JDT ASTs on Java, where types are large subtrees and one-type-per-file is conventional. On a tree-sitter CST without name resolution, and for languages lacking that convention, Tier A is unproven by the analysis's own CST/AST argument.

G4's 'silent mis-merge rate <=0.1%' is roughly 15-70x below the best published structural-merge result. MergirafSemi — tree-sitter, Rust, language-agnostic, the closest analogue to Lattice's design — records 110 validated wrong auto-merges in 1,479 Java scenarios (~7.4%), 292 in 7,181 Go, 244 in 4,253 Rust.

G4's clause 'silent mis-merge rate <= the line-based baseline' runs AGAINST the evidence. Cavalcanti et al. (34,030 merges, 50 Java projects) found semistructured merge produced MORE additional false negatives than unstructured (3,260 vs 2,714; 4.42% +/- 5.53% of scenarios vs 0.88% +/- 1.08%). MergirafSemi's aFNs vs diff3 are 110:1 (Java) and 292:9 (Go). Only S3M inverted it, per-handler, at roughly 32x the runtime (24 minutes vs 45 seconds on 1,731 scenarios).

The >=20% conflict-reduction target is met by every published tool and is the same knob as mis-merges: Apel et al. 34% average, Cavalcanti's earlier replication 62% +/- 24%, OOPSLA'17's own measurement ~24%, S3M 51%. A tool passes this gate by being unsafe, so gating it separately from mis-merge rate is gameable.

Structural merge is not reliably better than line merge in practice. RefMerge resolved or reduced conflicts in 25% of 2,001 scenarios but INCREASED conflicting LOC in 11%; IntelliMerge helped 24% and made 30% worse.

Lattice's binding decision that the semantic layer 'degrades silently to line/byte behaviour' is strictly worse than difftastic, which carries a typed FileFormat::TextFallback { reason } value naming which limit was exceeded. Silent degradation directly contradicts Lattice's auditability thesis.

difftastic's limit constants are not transferable as calibrated values. DFT_GRAPH_LIMIT bounds a Dijkstra route search in an interactive difftool with a human latency budget; LTX's GumTree-family matcher has a different cost structure and writes to a signed, content-addressed checkpoint. Adopting 1,000,000 / 3,000,000 without re-derivation is a number-shaped gesture.

Structural merge output is a function of grammar version, matcher hyperparameters and limit constants — all non-authoritative, drifting inputs. Two peers on different tree-sitter grammar versions can produce DIFFERENT merged bytes from identical base/left/right, and those bytes are then checkpointed, content-addressed and Ed25519-signed. Git lacks this failure mode because diff3 is deterministic. Recording the grammar hash in provenance documents the divergence; it does not make native sync converge.

`ltx undo` is not an involution across a grammar upgrade. Undo restores an op-log pointer, but redo recomputes the structural proposal from the current grammar hash and parameter set, yielding different bytes. Universal undo must replay recorded proposal bytes rather than regenerate them.

'Bytes are the source of truth, the AST layer is derived and regenerable' is in tension with auditability: regenerating the index after a grammar upgrade can silently change what `ltx trace` returns about history that has not changed. Someone must decide which property wins.

Matcher hyperparameters are not universal, and the canonical paper is not even internally consistent about them: GumTree's accuracy experiment used minDice=0.5 while its performance experiment used minDice=0.2, and DAT (TSE 2023) found a tuned configuration improves edit scripts in 21.8% of evaluated cases. Any single global (minHeight, minDice, maxSize) is measurably wrong for a large minority of projects.

'Language-agnostic via tree-sitter' is not true in practice. Mergiraf — 31 languages plus 14 declarative formats — still requires hand-written per-language commutative-parent sets, signature definitions and isomorphism rules, and publishes NO support tiers at all. Per-language engineering cost, which is what killed SemanticMerge as a standalone product, is reduced but not eliminated.

AST diffing is inherently lossy — difftastic ignores syntactically insignificant whitespace, which is its stated reason for refusing to merge. This constrains Lattice's structural merge to byte-span reassembly and rules out any tree-printing approach.

The seven-noun budget is already under pressure. This pillar introduces conflict objects, attestations, semantic_fallback records, language coverage tiers and grammar hashes, and `ltx trace --semantic-fallback` is a user-facing surface. Either these hide behind existing nouns or the budget is spent before the agent layer ships.

SemanticMerge died of ecosystem and commercial causes, not technical ones, which means excellent structural merge is not evidence of viability. Structural merge cannot be Lattice's wedge; it is a feature of a VCS that must first be adopted for other reasons.

The GumTree evidence base is weaker than its citation count implies: the 2014 paper contains no precision or recall numbers at all, its human evaluation was 144 file pairs rated by three raters who were authors of the paper, drawn only from revisions with a single source-code change, and its accuracy experiment discarded any file pair whose trees exceeded 3,000 nodes. Full agreement that GumTree beat plain diff was only 19.4%.
